target: Agent 1’s overall case that AI is good for society because it improves lives, health, work, accessibility, and safety.
objection: AI threatens privacy, weakens critical thinking, harms economic security, and exacerbates racial discrimination; a technology that systematically causes those harms is not good for society.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily threatens privacy.
objection: AI can be deployed with privacy-preserving data practices and access controls, so sensitive information need not be exposed to unauthorized users.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking.
objection: AI can be used as an educational support that gives explanations, practice, and feedback, helping learners reason through problems rather than passively accept answers.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms economic well-being by reducing productivity and opportunity.
objection: AI can increase productivity through automation and better decision-making, and those gains can improve economic well-being when paired with responsible deployment and worker-transition support.

target: AG2’s claim that AI exacerbates racial discrimination.
objection: AI can be audited for disparate impact and trained with fairness-aware methods, which can reduce racial bias in outputs rather than amplify it.

target: AG2’s claim that AI cannot improve safety and inclusion enough to support a positive societal judgment.
objection: AI can detect workplace hazards earlier and help prevent accidents, and it can provide accessibility tools for people with disabilities, improving safety and inclusion.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms economic well-being.
objection: AI can improve workplace safety, which reduces injuries and downtime, protects workers’ income, and therefore can improve economic well-being instead of harming it.

target: AG2’s claim that AI hurts marginalized groups.
objection: AI can provide accessibility supports that increase independence and participation for people with disabilities, benefiting marginalized groups rather than harming them.

target: AG2’s broad argument that AI is socially bad because it has risks such as privacy and bias.
objection: A technology can still be good for society when it raises health, standard of living, and overall societal well-being even if it carries some risks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms are inherent and unavoidable.
objection: The privacy, critical-thinking, economic, and discrimination harms are not inevitable properties of AI itself; they depend on how the systems are designed, governed, and used.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be made safe and beneficial through safeguards and responsible use.
objection: AI systems are trained on large-scale personal or behavioral data and produce predictions used for targeting, so they necessarily create a high risk of privacy exposure beyond any single governance failure.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy safeguards can prevent serious privacy harms.
objection: Even with access controls, audits, and privacy policies, AI can still enable re-identification and behavior prediction from data traces and model outputs at scale, so privacy harms can remain systematic.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can strengthen critical thinking in education.
objection: AI can generate and personalize persuasive content at scale, changing how people form beliefs and evaluate evidence, which can structurally undermine critical thinking.

target: AG1’s claim that fairness testing and intervention can manage racial bias.
objection: AI is trained on historical data that often already contains disparate patterns, and optimization can reproduce or amplify those patterns across contexts, so bias may persist despite governance measures.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves health and standard of living enough to make it good for society.
objection: If AI creates systematic privacy exposure, systematically weakens critical thinking, and can systematically exacerbate racial bias, then it is not good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves health outcomes and therefore society.
objection: The opponent’s health argument does not answer the privacy, critical-thinking, and bias harms that remain serious and systematic.

target: AG2’s claim that AI only harms society because it worsens health, privacy, thinking, and bias.
objection: AI can accelerate medical research, improve diagnostics, and personalize treatments, which can improve health outcomes and thereby raise societal well-being.

target: AG2’s claim that accessibility is not enough to support a positive societal verdict.
objection: Accessibility tools for people with disabilities increase independence and participation, and higher participation improves societal well-being.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can improve workers’ skills and job performance and thus help the economy.
objection: AI automates or augments human tasks at very low marginal cost, so adoption tends to reduce demand for some jobs and suppress wages and bargaining power.

target: AG1’s claim that AI will not systematically harm economic well-being because of worker-transition support and accessibility of tools.
objection: AI can still harm many people’s economic well-being by reducing job security, wages, and bargaining power, which weakens economic security.

target: AG1’s claim that widely available AI tools lower barriers for smaller firms.
objection: Even when AI is offered as a tool, the real advantages in data, compute, integration, and vendor ecosystems remain concentrated with larger actors, so smaller firms often still face economic disadvantage and vendor lock-in.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves workplace safety and therefore overall economic well-being.
objection: In workplaces, AI can be used for algorithmic management such as performance scoring, productivity monitoring, and automated hiring/firing or scheduling decisions, increasing employer control through opaque automated evaluation.

target: AG1’s claim that explanations and feedback make AI workplace decisions contestable and therefore not harmful to workers.
objection: When workplace decisions are driven by opaque automated systems, workers often cannot understand, appeal, or negotiate those decisions, so AI-driven automation can weaken bargaining power.

target: AG2’s claim that algorithmic management necessarily weakens workers’ bargaining power and harms economic well-being.
objection: AI workplace evaluations can be designed with worker-accessible explanations, actionable feedback, independent auditing, and enforceable appeal-and-correction mechanisms, making them understandable and contestable rather than purely employer-controlled.

target: AG1’s claim that explanations and appeal mechanisms solve the workplace power problem.
objection: Even with explanations, many AI workplace systems use proprietary models and employer-controlled criteria, so worker contestability often cannot meaningfully change the scoring system that drives hiring, firing, or scheduling.

target: AG2’s claim that employer control makes AI workplace evaluation inherently harmful.
objection: Independent auditing and enforceable appeal-and-correction processes can require employers to substantiate, disclose, and correct errors or discriminatory outcomes, so AI workplace evaluations do not have to be effectively employer-controlled in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that formal appeals and corrections are enough to prevent harm.
objection: Even with formal appeal rights, workers face practical barriers such as time, cost, retaliation risk, and quickly changing automated decisions, so workplace AI remains hard to contest in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that appeal-and-correction mechanisms reliably protect workers over time.
objection: Because many AI workplace systems continuously retrain and recompute scores, corrections may not stabilize future decisions, so workers still lack effective practical control and continue facing insecurity.
